1:
What the opening words announce is agreed on all hands. Gill takes the chapter for Adam's descent through Seth to Noah, ten generations only, with nothing of Cain's line or the collateral branches. Henry calls the phrase the title of the whole chapter, a catalogue not of all Adam's posterity but of the holy seed, the names and ages and deaths of those who succeeded the first Adam in the custody of the promise and were ancestors of the second; Wesley repeats him. Clarke observes that the Hebrew rendered book means a register, any kind of writing, even a bill of divorce, and takes it for the record reaching to the five hundredth year of Noah's life. Calvin reads it as a catalogue too, and states its purpose: to show that in the prodigious multitude of men there was always a number, however small, who worshipped God, preserved by celestial guardianship lest his name be obliterated and the seed of the Church fail. Keil and Delitzsch draw the same conclusion from an absence. The ages given here are withheld from the Cainite list, so this genealogy is at once a line of development and a chronology, the accursed family having no future history and needing no reckoning of years.

Why the creation account should be rehearsed at this point divides two of the commentators sharply. Clarke thinks it introduced to keep man in mind of the glory from which he fell, and to prove that the miseries and death of his present state came from his transgression and not his original condition; made in God's image, he was made free of natural and moral evil, and since the deaths of the patriarchs are now to be recited it was necessary to preface them so, to justify the ways of God to man. Ellicott takes the repetition to prove nearly the opposite. Man is fallen, but the words recur to show the divine likeness was not lost, nor the blessing given at his creation revoked; since that likeness does not mainly consist in moral innocence, it was untouched by sin except so far as sin corrupted the vessel holding the gift. Henry draws four lessons from the same verses: that God made man, who is therefore not his own master, the Author of his being being also the centre of his motions; that there was a day on which he was made, so he is the junior of the creation; that he was made righteous and holy, and therefore happy; and that they were made male and female for mutual comfort as well as increase. Wesley presses the fourth further, that both were made immediately by God's hand and both in his likeness, so between the sexes there is not the inequality some imagine; and where earthly parents can only beg a blessing, it is God's prerogative to command one.

Calvin finds in the one name given the pair a commendation of marriage, posterity learning to cherish the bond the more sacredly on seeing their first parents called by a single name; he dismisses as trifling the Jewish inference that married persons are therefore called Adam. Gill notes there was one male and one female only, the woman made after the man and out of him, though both on the same day. The turn from that likeness to Seth's is Keil's point. Adam was made in God's image and begat in his own, passing on what he had received, but not in its original purity: it came down in the form his own self-determination had given it, modified and corrupted by sin. Keil marks too the formula that now begins, the years before the son, the other sons and daughters, the sum of the years, and last the words and he died, which looks superfluous but by its constant recurrence shows that death reigned from Adam downward as an unchangeable law.
4:
Gill insists the years are solar, not lunar, against Varro, reckoning them at three hundred and sixty-five days and odd hours after the Egyptian usage of Moses's time. He argues from the absurdities of the alternative: on a shorter year Enoch must have begotten a son in his sixth year, several lives would fall below our own, and the interval between creation and deluge would shrink to two hundred years. He supports the long lives from outside Scripture too, citing heathen writers who say the ancients lived a thousand years, a round number for their longevity, and noting Josephus appeals to Manetho and Berosus. Ellicott is less confident about the figures themselves. The numbers of the Bible are involved in great difficulty, since Hebrew numeration attaches values to letters and adds them, and the words so formed, being unmeaning, are easily corrupted; hence the three authorities differ widely on the interval from the expulsion out of Paradise to the flood, the Hebrew making it 1656 years, the Samaritan 1307 and the Greek 2262, while agreeing almost everywhere on the length of the individual lives. Ellicott finds an appearance of untrustworthiness about the Greek calculations and ranks the Samaritan nearly equal in authority with the Hebrew, noting that Jerome knew Samaritan copies agreeing with the Hebrew and none such survive. Gill sees the same hand in the smaller discrepancy here, the Greek adding a hundred years before Seth's birth and taking them off afterwards to keep the total right.

Ellicott will not leave the matter as a mere textual problem. Whatever the figures, the Bible plainly represents human life as vastly prolonged before the flood and rapidly shortening after, and teaches that in the Messianic age life shall be prolonged again, a century being the length of childhood and a grown man's age as the age of a tree. Against that he sets what the physiologists say, that man being what he now is, a hundred and twenty to a hundred and fifty years is the utmost possible term. Calvin looks at what the overlapping lives allowed. Through six successive ages, when the family of Seth had grown into a great people, the voice of Adam might daily resound among them, renewing the memory of the creation, the fall and the punishment, testifying to the hope of salvation left after chastisement, and reciting the judgments of God for the instruction of all. After his death his sons might hand on what they had learned, but instruction from the mouth of the eyewitness was far more forcible; and Calvin ends on the failure of it, that so wonderful and even monstrous was the general obstinacy that not even the sounder part of mankind could be held to the obedience and fear of God.

On the closing words Calvin denies that they are superfluous. They warn us that death was not denounced against men in vain, and that we lie under the curse to which man was doomed unless deliverance is had elsewhere; we are to reflect on our condition, in which the image of God is destroyed, or at least obliterated, and we scarcely retain the faint shadow of a life from which we hasten to death. It is useful, he says, in a picture of so many ages, to see at one glance the continual course of divine vengeance, since otherwise we imagine God has forgotten, and to nothing are we more prone than to dream of an immortality on earth unless death is often set before our eyes. Wesley pushes the sentence back to its cause. In the day Adam ate the forbidden fruit he became mortal and began to die, so his whole life afterwards was a forfeited and condemned life, and more, a wasting and dying one; he was not merely like a criminal under sentence but like one already crucified, who dies slowly and by degrees.
6:
Five names pass with nothing told of them, and Henry makes the silence his subject. All the Holy Ghost thought fit to record of Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel and Jared is their ages, though we have reason to think them men of eminence for prudence and piety. Why is so little said at such length? Henry answers that it might have been delivered in fewer words, but there is not one idle word in God's books, whatever there is in men's. He gives two reasons. The first is condescension to the meanest capacity: a little arithmetic would carry a reader from the age at the son's birth and the years lived after to the sum of a life, yet the total is set down for those without even so much skill. The second is the pleasure God takes in his people's names. Cain's line was numbered in haste; this account of the holy seed is enlarged and given in words at length rather than figures, so we are told how long those lived who lived in God's fear and when those died who died in his favour, while as for the rest it is no matter. The memory of the just is blessed, Henry closes, but the name of the wicked shall rot. Wesley reproduces the passage.

What Wesley adds is a meditation on the length of the lives. Not one died before he had seen almost eight hundred years, and some a great deal more, which he calls a long while for an immortal soul to be imprisoned in a house of clay. Two inferences follow. The present life cannot have been the burden to them it commonly is now, or they would have grown weary of it; and the life to come was not revealed as clearly as under the gospel, or they would have been impatient to be gone. Wesley will assign natural causes too, thinking it probable that before the flood the earth was more fruitful, its produce more strengthening, the air more healthful and the influences of the heavenly bodies more benign. Ellicott finds in these short intervals a proof about the calendar. The years cannot have been revolutions of the moon, as some suppose, since Enos was ninety at his son's birth, Cainan seventy and Mahalaleel sixty-five; the supposition would sit better on the Greek text, where no patriarch has a son before his hundred and sixty-second year.

Gill explains why only one son is ever named. Enos was surely not Seth's firstborn, and no doubt there were children before him, but he alone is named because the line ran through him from Adam to Noah, the father of the new world, from whom the Messiah was to spring; to give that descent is the principal view of the book. The rest of Gill's notes are textual: the Greek makes Enos a hundred and ninety at Cainan's birth, and at Jared it agrees with the Hebrew while the Samaritan reads only sixty-two, which Gill thinks can hardly have been the age at a first son. Ellicott treats the last name at more length and with more caution. Jared is supposed to mean descent, particularly of water, and many have tried on that ground to identify him with the Indian water-god, though competent modern commentators regard such Aryan expositions as exploded; Sayce reports the word means servant in Assyrian, which Ellicott does not find satisfactory either, and until that dialect is thoroughly explored he thinks we can scarcely speak with certainty about these names. He does draw one inference from the figure. Jared was a hundred and sixty-two at Enoch's birth, which makes it probable Enoch was not the eldest son but came into the birthright by his own excellencies; and he stands seventh from Adam, seven being the number of perfection, reaches the highest rank of these patriarchs, and passes into immortality without dying.
21:
Henry marks the change of pace. The accounts have run on for generations with nothing to distinguish them but names and numbers, and then comes one not to be passed over: Enoch, the seventh from Adam. The rest, we may suppose, did virtuously, but he excelled them all and was the brightest star of the patriarchal age, and though little is recorded it is enough to make his name greater than the other Enoch's. Calvin sharpens it by an objection. Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel and Jared were all living, their piety celebrated a few verses earlier, so the age cannot have been barbarous with so many excellent teachers; from which he infers that the probity of the man whom the Spirit exempted from the common order was rare and almost singular. Gill fastens on the son's name as a prophecy: on Bochart's derivation Methuselah means that when he dies there shall be a sending forth of waters to destroy the earth.

What walking with God means is expounded most fully by Henry, whom Wesley follows almost word for word. It denotes true religion, for what is godliness but walking with God? The profane are without God and walk contrary to him, while the godly walk with him, which presupposes reconciliation, since two cannot walk together except they be agreed. It is to set him always before us and act as men under his eye, to live in communion with him, and to make his word our rule and his glory our end; Wesley adds that it is to comply with his will and be a worker together with him. Both notice that the phrase begins after Methuselah's birth, Wesley taking it that Enoch grew eminent for piety only then, while Gill supposes he had walked with God before but now more closely, and held on despite the apostasy that began in his father's days. Clarke goes to the words. Enoch signifies to instruct or dedicate, from which he judges the man was early taught the things of God; and the Hebrew verb stands in a form denoting what a man does upon himself, so Enoch set himself to walk, fixedly purposed not to receive the grace of God in vain. Calvin draws the practical lesson, that here is the way to escape the manners of those we live among, since public custom is a violent tempest, men following the multitude and assuming that whatever is commonly received must be lawful; no contagion, he says, is worse than evil example.

The ending is what all of them dwell on. Ellicott observes that the Greek renders it Enoch pleased God, whence the testimony quoted in Hebrews, the Hebrew giving the cause of which the Greek names the effect. In place of the mournful refrain closing every other life here, which comes each time like a surprise after so many years, there is an early removal into another world without pain or decay, suggesting that long life was not the highest blessing; so one of Adam's posterity after the fall achieved, not without special help, what Adam in Paradise had failed to do. He adds that the removal fell about the middle of the antediluvian period, and that Enoch's age was three hundred and sixty-five, the number of days in a year. Calvin will have no such softening. A man must be shamelessly contentious, he says, who will not acknowledge something extraordinary here: all are taken out of the world by death, but Moses declares that Enoch went by an unusual mode and was received miraculously, as Elijah afterwards was. In it an example of immortality was exhibited, designed, Calvin thinks, to raise the faith of the saints before their own death and mitigate their dread of it; and he remarks with feeling that Adam was denied this comfort, having nothing in his ears but the sentence that he should die the death.
25:
Methuselah's name is read as a prophecy, his father having been a prophet. Henry and Wesley take it for he dies, or there is a sending forth of the deluge, which came in the very year he died; and whether or not it was so intended, this much is observable: the longest liver who ever was carried death about in his name, that he might be minded of its coming surely though it came slowly. On the age both turn the same way: nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and yet he died, for the longest liver must die at last, and neither youth nor age discharges from that war. Clarke is more cautious: this is the longest life mentioned in Scripture and probably the longest ever lived, though we have no authority to say so; and of a man who came within thirty-one years of a thousand it is still written that he died. Yet he will not call life a misfortune: uncertain and full of evils as it is, it is a blessing in all its periods if devoted to the glory of God and the interest of the soul.

Gill gives the Jewish reason why no man reached the round figure, that a thousand years is God's day and none may arrive at it. Henry supposes he died shortly before the flood, taken away from the evil to come; but he enters a scruple. All this presumes that every patriarch named here was a holy and good man; Henry is loth to surmise the contrary, yet does not see that it can be inferred merely from their enrolment among the ancestors of Christ. Gill observes that Seth's line repeats names from Cain's, Lamech here and Enoch before.

With Noah the chapter turns from dying to hoping, and Henry hears in the naming a complaint and an expectation. The complaint is of the calamitous state of human life, since by sin and the entail of the curse our life is spent in labour; God having cursed the ground, it is as much as some men can do to fetch a hard livelihood out of it. Lamech speaks, Henry says, as one fatigued with the business of life, grudging that so many precious minutes must go to the support of the body. The expectation is in the words this same shall comfort us, which carry more than a parent's ordinary wish that a child prove a help; Henry thinks some prophecy probably lay behind it. On the name Gill joins the two ideas, that rest gives comfort and comfort flows from rest. Clarke separates them and chooses: some derive Noah from a root meaning to comfort, but he thinks it likelier to come from one meaning to rest, and asks what is more comfortable than rest after toil. Calvin settles the philology against the first: the verb meaning to comfort does not answer to the noun meaning rest unless a letter be called superfluous, and the name comes from the latter, so Lamech's words are either a transmutation of letters or a bare allusion. He asks besides how a father could hope so much from a son whose disposition he could not yet have discerned, and answers with the Jews that the saying was a prophecy, faulting them only for restricting to agriculture what belongs to all human misery. Ellicott adds the bleakest note in the chapter: this is the first child since Eve's day recorded as named at birth, and in both cases the name ended in disappointment, for Noah brought no rest, and in his days came the flood. He reads them as spoken prophetically of the man who built the ark, and takes him for a typical person, since after the waters dried God smelled a savour of rest and said he would not curse the ground again.
32:
Why Noah had no son until his five hundredth year is asked by three commentators and answered three ways. Gill can hardly think he lived so long childless, and supposes he may have had children who died; but he reports the view that Providence ordered it so, since God meant to save this household and an earlier start might have given him more than the ark could hold. Ellicott says flatly that no reason is given, and that it does not follow Noah had no other sons, only that any such were unworthy to share the deliverance; he thinks it remarkable too that none of the three in the ark had children until after the flood. Calvin dismisses the pious reading outright. Those err, he thinks, who find Noah's chastity proclaimed here because he passed nearly five centuries unmarried, for the text neither says he was unmarried till then nor tells when he first became a father; Moses is naming the time he was warned of the deluge, and adds that about then he was father of three sons, not that he had them already but because they were born not long after.

The order of the three names is agreed to be one of dignity, not birth. Gill works the dates out: Ham was the younger, and since Shem was a hundred two years after the flood he must have been born in the five hundred and second year, so Japheth was probably the eldest. Clarke reaches the same result from the tenth chapter and from Chronicles, and states the principle governing such lists, that where Scripture marks precedency the favoured son is put first though younger, as Jacob before Esau and Ephraim before Manasseh; what he cannot account for is why Ham, the youngest and by the next chapter the worst, should appear out of his natural order. Wesley gives the reason for Shem's place: the covenant was entailed on him, God being afterwards called the Lord God of Shem, and from him both Christ the head and the church the body descend. His very name means a name, because in his posterity the name of God should remain until he came whose name is above every name; so in putting Shem first, Wesley says, Christ was in effect put first, who in all things must have the pre-eminence. Ellicott glosses the other names too, Ham the dark-coloured, ancestor of the Egyptians and Cushites, and Japheth the widener, or on another account the fair, who though youngest fathered most of the races of Europe and some nations of Asia. Calvin declines to say whether the earlier men were firstborn, since Moses meant only to follow the succession of the Church, and observes that God, to keep men from a vain confidence in the flesh, often chooses those who come later in nature's order.

Clarke closes by standing back. Of all these patriarchs the best was on earth the shortest time: Enoch's years were exactly the days of a solar revolution, and like the sun he ran a glorious course, shining more and more unto the perfect day and taken away in his meridian splendour. From the computation Clarke draws two more observations: that Adam lived to see Lamech in the ninth generation and died in the fifty-sixth year of that man's life, being the first who lived, the first who sinned and the first to taste death naturally, Abel's being violent; and that Enoch was taken next after Adam, leaving seven patriarchs as witnesses of his translation. Wesley looks forward instead, explaining why the account of the old world's degeneracy is set down so fully before the story of its ruin: for the glory of God's justice and for warning to a wicked world, since destroying it was no act of absolute sovereignty but of necessary justice, maintaining the honour of God's government.
